claim: The Drosophila embryonic hindgut first forms as a bilaterally symmetric structure and then rotates 90° counterclockwise as viewed from the posterior, showing dextral looping.
source: An in vivo function of cell chirality was first discovered in the Drosophila embryonic hindgut (Taniguchi et al., 2011), which first forms as a bilaterally symmetric structure and then rotates 90° counterclockwise as viewed from the posterior, showing dextral looping (Hozumi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Taniguchi et al., 2011; Hozumi et al., 2006).

claim: The posterior end of the hindgut does not rotate, and thus the hindgut twists as a whole.
source: The posterior end of the hindgut does not rotate, and thus the hindgut twists as a whole.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the manuscript.

claim: The hindgut epithelial cells are probably responsible for hindgut rotation, since the LR defect in hindgut rotation in mutants is fully rescued when the responsible genes are expressed specifically in hindgut epithelial cells.
source: The hindgut epithelial cells are probably responsible for this rotation, since the LR defect in hindgut rotation in mutants is fully rescued when the responsible genes are expressed specifically in hindgut epithelial cells (Hozumi et al., 2006; Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing rescue experiments.

claim: Before the directional rotation begins, the hindgut epithelial cells exhibit an LR asymmetric shape of their apical surface with respect to the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Before the directional rotation begins, the anterior-posterior axis of the hindgut can be defined, because its simple tubular structure extends in the anterior-posterior direction, and the hindgut epithelial cells exhibit an LR asymmetric shape of their apical surface with respect to the anterior-posterior axis (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The LR asymmetric shape of hindgut epithelial cells eventually disappears and the cells become symmetric after the rotation.
source: The LR asymmetric shape eventually disappears and the cells become symmetric after the rotation (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A previous computer simulation showed that the introduction and subsequent dissolution of cell chirality are sufficient to induce the rotation of a model epithelial tube.
source: A previous computer simulation showed that the introduction and subsequent dissolution of cell chirality are sufficient to induce the rotation of a model epithelial tube (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During the rotation, neither cell proliferation nor cell death occurs in the hindgut.
source: During the rotation, neither cell proliferation nor cell death occurs in the hindgut (Lengyel and Iwaki, 2002; Wells et al., 2013), indicating that cell-shape changes and/or cell rearrangements are involved in this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell-shape changes and/or cell rearrangements are involved in hindgut rotation.
source: During the rotation, neither cell proliferation nor cell death occurs in the hindgut (Lengyel and Iwaki, 2002; Wells et al., 2013), indicating that cell-shape changes and/or cell rearrangements are involved in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of cell proliferation and death.

claim: Cell chirality drives the counterclockwise rotation of the hindgut.
source: Together, these observations indicate that cell chirality drives the counterclockwise rotation of the hindgut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: An explanted wild-type hindgut rotated counterclockwise in vitro.
source: Here, we found that an explanted wild-type hindgut rotated counterclockwise in vitro, confirming that the hindgut itself generates an active force to accomplish the rotation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hindgut itself generates an active force to accomplish the rotation.
source: Here, we found that an explanted wild-type hindgut rotated counterclockwise in vitro, confirming that the hindgut itself generates an active force to accomplish the rotation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that explanted hindguts rotate in vitro.

claim: Of the explanted hindguts, 85% (11 out of 13) showed normal counterclockwise rotation.
source: Of the explanted hindguts, 85% (11 out of 13) showed normal counterclockwise rotation.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the explant culture experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hindgut started to rotate at late embryonic stage 12, when the germ band was almost completely retracted.
source: The hindgut started to rotate at late embryonic stage 12, when the germ band was almost completely retracted (Figure 1A1).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging data shown in Figure 1A1.

claim: The hindgut twisted 90° counterclockwise, and this rotation was fully complete by 2 hr.
source: The hindgut twisted 90° counterclockwise, and this rotation was fully complete by 2 hr (Figures 1A1–3, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging data shown in Figures 1A1-3.

claim: Cells changed their position relative to the cells located below them (posterior in the embryo) by sliding leftward on the dorsal side of the hindgut.
source: Using time-laps movies, we tracked cells located in the dorsal side of the hindgut by their nuclear position in individual time frames (5 min intervals) (red boxes in Figure 1B). The cells changed their position relative to the cells located below them (posterior in the embryo) by sliding leftward (Figures 1C1–3, Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging data shown in Figures 1C1-3.

claim: The displacement of wild-type epithelial cells in the dorsal side was about −0.5 μm, indicating that the cells moved significantly leftward in relation to their subjacent neighbors.
source: The displacement of wild-type epithelial cells in the dorsal side was about −0.5 μm, indicating that the cells moved significantly leftward in relation to their subjacent neighbors (Figure 1F, dorsal).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cells on the ventral side of the hindgut showed a significant opposite directional movement compared to dorsal cells.
source: Although we could only obtain data from low numbers of cells because most images of the deep ventral region gave poor signals, even using two-photon microscopy, the results revealed a significant opposite directional movement of cells on the ventral side (Figure 1F, ventral).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: During the counterclockwise rotation of the hindgut, cells change their position relative to their subjacent cells (posterior neighbors) by sliding in the direction of rotation.
source: These results together suggested that during the counterclockwise rotation of the hindgut, cells change their position relative to their subjacent cells (posterior neighbors) by sliding in the direction of rotation (Figure 1C,D,F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell tracking data shown in Figures 1C, D, and F.

claim: In Myo31DF mutants, the LR asymmetry of various organs is reversed.
source: In Myo31DF mutants, the LR asymmetry of various organs is reversed (Hozumi et al., 2006; Spéder et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More than 80% of the Myo31DF embryos showed inverted hindgut rotation, with sinistral looping.
source: More than 80% of the Myo31DF embryos showed inverted hindgut rotation, with sinistral looping (Figures 2A1–3, Figure 2—video 1) (Hozumi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is data from observations of Myo31DF mutants, supported by citation and shown in Figures 2A1-3.

claim: In Myo31DF mutants, the cell chirality of the hindgut epithelial cells before the onset of rotation is inverted.
source: In Myo31DF mutants, the cell chirality of the hindgut epithelial cells before the onset of rotation is also inverted (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The chirality of Myo31DF cells is determined cell-autonomously.
source: Furthermore, the chirality of Myo31DF cells is determined cell-autonomously (Hatori et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hindgut epithelial cells in Myo31DF mutants changed their relative position by sliding rightward, which is the opposite direction to that observed in wild-type cells.
source: We found that these cells changed their relative position by sliding rightward, which is the opposite direction to that observed in the wild-type cells (Figures 2B1–3, Figure 2—video 2), and the ventral cells slid to the left side (Figure 2C1 and , Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging data shown in Figures 2B1-3 and 2C1.

claim: Quantitative analysis confirmed that the cells on both the dorsal and ventral sides of the Myo31DF hindgut slid in a direction opposite to that of wild-type cells.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed that the cells on both the dorsal and ventral sides of the Myo31DF hindgut slid in a direction opposite to that of wild-type cells (Figure 2D, dorsal and ventral, cf. Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The direction of cell sliding is consistent with the rotation direction of the wild-type and Myo31DF hindgut.
source: These results showed that the direction of cell sliding is consistent with the rotation direction of the wild-type and Myo31DF hindgut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing cell sliding directions with rotation directions.

claim: The initial cell chirality appeared to determine the direction of the cell sliding.
source: Therefore, the initial cell chirality appeared to determine the direction of the cell sliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between cell chirality and sliding direction.

claim: Cells maintained their junctions during cell sliding in both the wild type and the Myo31DF mutant in most cases.
source: The results revealed that cells maintained their junctions during cell sliding in both the wild type and the Myo31DF mutant in most cases (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—video 1, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The frequency of cell-intercalation events accompanied by junctional remodeling was 9.2 and 6.0% for wild type and the Myo31DF mutant, respectively.
source: The frequency of cell-intercalation events accompanied by junctional remodeling was 9.2 and 6.0% for wild type and the Myo31DF mutant, respectively (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell intercalation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: More than 90% of the cell junctions were not remodeled during cell sliding.
source: Therefore, more than 90% of the cell junctions were not remodeled during cell sliding, suggesting that the cell sliding does not necessarily require junctional remodeling.
evidence: This is calculated from the frequency data in Table 1.

claim: Cell sliding does not necessarily require junctional remodeling.
source: Therefore, more than 90% of the cell junctions were not remodeled during cell sliding, suggesting that the cell sliding does not necessarily require junctional remodeling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency of junctional remodeling during cell sliding.

claim: The frequency of leftward versus rightward intercalations was similar in both the wild-type and Myo31DF hindguts.
source: The frequency of leftward versus rightward intercalations was similar in both the wild-type and Myo31DF hindguts (Table 1), indicating that the direction of cell intercalation during hindgut rotation does not have an LR bias.
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell intercalation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The direction of cell intercalation during hindgut rotation does not have an LR bias.
source: The frequency of leftward versus rightward intercalations was similar in both the wild-type and Myo31DF hindguts (Table 1), indicating that the direction of cell intercalation during hindgut rotation does not have an LR bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the intercalation frequency data in Table 1.

claim: In both the wild-type and Myo31DF hindgut, all of the diminishing cell boundaries had an angle with an absolute value less than 30°, and most of them were within ±10°.
source: In both the wild-type and Myo31DF hindgut, all of the diminishing cell boundaries had an angle with an absolute value less than 30°, and most of them were within ±10° (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell boundary angle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Cell intercalation does not have a major role in the LR directional rotation of the hindgut.
source: These results further indicated that cell intercalation does not have a major role in the LR directional rotation of the hindgut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of LR bias in cell intercalation.

claim: LR symmetrical cell intercalation contributes to elongation of the hindgut in the anterior-posterior direction through convergent extension.
source: Instead, this LR symmetrical cell intercalation contributes to elongation of the hindgut in the anterior-posterior direction through convergent extension (Iwaki and Lengyel, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: No clear anisotropy in the distribution of MyoII was detected in hindgut epithelial cells.
source: However, we failed to detect clear anisotropy in the distribution of MyoII (Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from live imaging of MyoII shown in Figure 3—video 3.

claim: The boundaries between cells aligned in a column tended to tilt in a ccw direction in wild type and in a cw direction in Myo31DF mutants during hindgut rotation.
source: The boundaries between cells aligned in a column tended to tilt in a ccw direction in wild type and in a cw direction in Myo31DF mutants during hindgut rotation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cell boundary angle analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cell sliding is accompanied by cell deformation associated with the dissolution of cell chirality.
source: These results suggested that cell sliding is accompanied by cell deformation associated with the dissolution of cell chirality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed cell boundary tilting during rotation.

claim: The model tube had twisted 88.5° at t = 80.0, forming a left-handed screw.
source: The tube had twisted 88.5° at t = 80.0, forming a left-handed screw (its tip was oriented anteriorly), which could be observed by coloring blue an array of cells that lined up straight along the anterior-posterior axis of the model gut tube before the twist and gradually became slanted during the twisting (Figure 4A, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is data from the computer simulation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 3D vertex model recapitulated chiral cell sliding that was associated with a loss of cell chirality.
source: Nevertheless, our 3D vertex model recapitulated chiral cell sliding that was associated with a loss of cell chirality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computer simulation results.

claim: In the early phases of the simulation, the polygons quickly became rounder or less polarized in shape, suggesting that the loss of chirality in the cell shape began even before the polygons started to prominently change their relative positions.
source: We found that in the early phases of the simulation, the polygons quickly became rounder or less polarized in shape, suggesting that the loss of chirality in the cell shape began even before the polygons started to prominently change their relative positions (Figure 4E, t = 1.0).
evidence: This is an observation from the computer simulation shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The loss of cell chirality began before the changes in the relative positions of the cells (called cell sliding in this study).
source: Thus, the loss of cell chirality began before the changes in the relative positions of the cells (called cell sliding in this study).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal sequence observed in the simulation.

claim: The time lag between the initiations of cell deformation and of cell sliding suggests that these two events were mechanically distinct, probably due to the different viscoelastic properties of individual cells versus cell aggregates in the model.
source: The time lag between the initiations of cell deformation and of cell sliding suggests that these two events were mechanically distinct, probably due to the different viscoelastic properties of individual cells versus cell aggregates in our model (Honda et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed time lag in the simulation, supported by citation.

claim: In a simulation where the vertices at the top and bottom of the tube were fixed, the polygons did not slide in one direction while the cell chirality was still lost.
source: In this simulation, the polygons did not slide in one direction (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), while the cell chirality was still lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C), indicating that the cell sliding or gut-tube rotation is not required for the loss of cell chirality.
evidence: This is data from a modified computer simulation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cell sliding or gut-tube rotation is not required for the loss of cell chirality.
source: In this simulation, the polygons did not slide in one direction (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), while the cell chirality was still lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C), indicating that the cell sliding or gut-tube rotation is not required for the loss of cell chirality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modified simulation results.

claim: The loss of cell chirality and the cell sliding are not always coupled.
source: These results also showed that the loss of cell chirality and the cell sliding are not always coupled, further suggesting that they are distinct mechanical events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modified simulation results.

claim: The mechanical force bias induced by cell chirality drives directional cell sliding and gut-tube rotation.
source: Therefore, this simulation further supported the idea that the mechanical force bias induced by cell chirality drives directional cell sliding and gut-tube rotation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The inverted rotation and cell sliding were recapitulated in a simulation with enantiomorphic chirality.
source: We found that the inverted rotation and cell sliding were recapitulated in this simulation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is data from a computer simulation with inverted chirality shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The initial cell chirality determines the direction of cell sliding.
source: These results supported the idea that the initial cell chirality determines the direction of cell sliding, as predicted in the in vivo studies above.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inverted chirality simulation results.

claim: Cell intercalation rarely occurred during the simulation (it occurred only 12 times for 452 vertices (2.7%) by t = 80).
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that cell intercalation rarely occurred during the simulation, although our model allowed for it [it occurred only 12 times for 452 vertices (2.7%) by t = 80]; for example, we did not observe any cell intercalation among the array of blue colored cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the computer simulation.

claim: In a computer simulation that did not allow junctional remodeling, the cells still slid and the tube rotated (twist angle 83.1° at t = 80).
source: To confirm that cell deformation rather than cell intercalation is a major driving force of the cell sliding and the hindgut rotation, we generated a computer simulation that did not allow junctional remodeling (Figure 4B). In this simulation, the cells still slid and the tube rotated (twist angle 83.1° at t = 80).
evidence: This is data from a modified computer simulation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cell sliding induced by a cell-chirality-provoked mechanical force bias is a dynamic cellular process connecting cell chirality and LR asymmetric tube twisting.
source: Thus, collectively, the simulations indicated that cell sliding induced by a cell-chirality-provoked mechanical force bias is a dynamic cellular process connecting cell chirality and LR asymmetric tube twisting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computer simulation results.

claim: Cell sliding converts the intrinsic chirality of the cell shape into the LR asymmetric epithelial morphogenesis though chiral cell deformation.
source: In conclusion, our in vivo and in silico analyses both demonstrated that cell sliding converts the intrinsic chirality of the cell shape into the LR asymmetric epithelial morphogenesis though chiral cell deformation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from both in vivo and in silico analyses.

claim: In mice, a leftward flow of extraembryonic fluid, called nodal flow, is generated in the node by the clockwise rotation of cilia.
source: In mice, a leftward flow of extraembryonic fluid, called nodal flow, is generated in the node by the clockwise rotation of cilia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate LR asymmetry.

claim: The nodal flow breaks the LR symmetry and eventually induces left-side-specific gene expressions, including Nodal, Lefty, and Pitx-2, the so-called nodal cassette genes.
source: The nodal flow breaks the LR symmetry and eventually induces left-side-specific gene expressions, including Nodal, Lefty, and Pitx-2, the so-called nodal cassette genes (Nonaka et al., 2002; Nonaka et al., 1998; Okada and Hirokawa, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It was recently reported that the LR asymmetric looping of the zebrafish heart develops by a tissue-intrinsic mechanism, independent of nodal.
source: However, it was recently reported that the LR asymmetric looping of the zebrafish heart develops by a tissue-intrinsic mechanism, independent of nodal (Noël et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Many mammalian cell lines adopt an LR asymmetric shape when cultured on a micropattern.
source: Many mammalian cell lines adopt an LR asymmetric shape when cultured on a micropattern (Chen et al., 2012; Raymond et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2011; Worley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cultured zebrafish melanophores show chirality in cellular locomotion and in cytoplasm swirling.
source: Cultured zebrafish melanophores show chirality in cellular locomotion and in cytoplasm swirling (Yamanaka and Kondo, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fibroblasts from human foreskin seeded on a micropattern exhibit a chiral swirling of actin fibers.
source: Fibroblasts from human foreskin seeded on a micropattern exhibit a chiral swirling of actin fibers (Tee et al., 2015), and cultured neutrophils show LR-biased movement in the absence of positional cues (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cultured neutrophils show LR-biased movement in the absence of positional cues.
source: Fibroblasts from human foreskin seeded on a micropattern exhibit a chiral swirling of actin fibers (Tee et al., 2015), and cultured neutrophils show LR-biased movement in the absence of positional cues (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The physiological roles of cell chirality in vertebrates remain unknown.
source: However, the physiological roles of cell chirality in vertebrates remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Cell intercalation is known to be required for the convergent extension of the hindgut.
source: Cell intercalation is known to be required for the convergent extension of the hindgut (Johansen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cell chirality was observed before the hindgut rotation and was lost during the rotation in vivo.
source: Considering that cell chirality was observed before the hindgut rotation and was lost during the rotation in vivo, the cancelation of cell chirality is probably a primary driving force for the subsequent events including the cell sliding and hindgut rotation, in vivo.
evidence: This is an observation from in vivo studies.

claim: The cancelation of cell chirality is probably a primary driving force for the subsequent events including the cell sliding and hindgut rotation, in vivo.
source: Considering that cell chirality was observed before the hindgut rotation and was lost during the rotation in vivo, the cancelation of cell chirality is probably a primary driving force for the subsequent events including the cell sliding and hindgut rotation, in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of events observed in vivo.

claim: Explanted linear hearts of various species develop dextral looping in culture.
source: Moreover, explanted linear hearts of various species develop dextral looping in culture (Bacon, 1945; Manning and McLachlan, 1990; Noël et al., 2013), suggesting that the heart LR asymmetry formation is tissue-intrinsic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The heart LR asymmetry formation is tissue-intrinsic.
source: Moreover, explanted linear hearts of various species develop dextral looping in culture (Bacon, 1945; Manning and McLachlan, 1990; Noël et al., 2013), suggesting that the heart LR asymmetry formation is tissue-intrinsic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that explanted hearts develop asymmetry in culture.

claim: In Drosophila, various organs use cell chirality as a common strategy to establish LR asymmetry in a tissue-intrinsic manner, in the absence of an LR body axis.
source: In Drosophila, which lacks the Nodal cassette gene functions, various organs use cell chirality as a common strategy to establish LR asymmetry in a tissue-intrinsic manner, in the absence of an LR body axis (González-Morales et al., 2015; Sato et al., 2015a; Taniguchi et al., 2011; Vorbrüggen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell chirality in tissues has been observed only in Drosophila to date.
source: To date, cell chirality in tissues has been observed only in Drosophila (González-Morales et al., 2015; Sato et al., 2015a; Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Cell chirality has been reported in cultured cells, including those of vertebrates.
source: However, cell chirality has been reported in cultured cells, including those of vertebrates (Chen et al., 2012; Raymond et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many cell types from various organs show a chiral cell shape.
source: Importantly, many cell types from various organs show a chiral cell shape (Chen et al., 2012; Raymond et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell chirality may play specific roles in the LR asymmetric organogenesis in vertebrates as well.
source: Therefore, cell chirality may play specific roles in the LR asymmetric organogenesis in vertebrates as well.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of cell chirality in vertebrate cells.

claim: Cell sliding is a novel mechanism driving epithelial morphogenesis, in which cells directionally change their position relative to their subjacent (posterior) neighbors by sliding in one direction.
source: Using live-imaging analysis and a three-dimensional vertex model, we identified 'cell sliding,' a novel mechanism driving epithelial morphogenesis, in which cells directionally change their position relative to their subjacent (posterior) neighbors by sliding in one direction.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by both in vivo and in silico data.

claim: In Drosophila embryonic hindgut, an initial left-right (LR) asymmetry of the cell shape (cell chirality in three dimensions), which occurs intrinsically before tissue deformation, is converted through LR asymmetric cell sliding into a directional axial twisting of the epithelial tube.
source: In Drosophila embryonic hindgut, an initial left-right (LR) asymmetry of the cell shape (cell chirality in three dimensions), which occurs intrinsically before tissue deformation, is converted through LR asymmetric cell sliding into a directional axial twisting of the epithelial tube.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by both in vivo and in silico data.

claim: In a Drosophila inversion mutant showing inverted cell chirality and hindgut rotation, cell sliding occurs in the opposite direction to that in wild-type.
source: In a Drosophila inversion mutant showing inverted cell chirality and hindgut rotation, cell sliding occurs in the opposite direction to that in wild-type.
evidence: This is a finding from the study of Myo31DF mutants, supported by in vivo data.

claim: Unlike directional cell intercalation, cell sliding does not require junctional remodeling.
source: Unlike directional cell intercalation, cell sliding does not require junctional remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that most cell junctions are maintained during cell sliding.

claim: Cell sliding may also be involved in other cases of LR-polarized epithelial morphogenesis.
source: Cell sliding may also be involved in other cases of LR-polarized epithelial morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.
